segments.line: One p. m.
You and Mo jump into the back of a taxi.
'Follow that car! ' you shout.
The driver looks at you in the mirror. 'Which car? '
You point at a random blue one. He shrugs and follows it.
For twenty minutes. Straight to a grocery store.
'That, ' he says, 'was the most boring car chase of my life. '
The meter says thirty- eight dollars.
In the game, you'd just jump out and run. So you do.
And this is where real life stops being a game.
Running off without paying a taxi fare is a crime in most places. It's called theft of services. It's in the same family as shoplifting.
And that car outside the bakery this morning? Police take that very seriously, because that's how a lot of car thefts start.
In the US, a car gets stolen about every thirty- two seconds. That's around a million cars a year. That's real.
The driver doesn't chase you. He doesn't need to. He has a dash camera, your face, and the exact spot where you got in.
Two p. m. Mo's video has fifty thousand views.
Somebody recognized your hoodie. The one still hanging on the neighbor's fence.
Three p. m. You run a red light on the scooter. A camera flashes.
In California, a red light ticket can cost close to five hundred dollars, once all the fees are added.
Four p. m. You add it up. The fence. The backyard. The scooter. The taxi. The car.
In the game, each of those is nothing. Real life keeps a list. And real life doesn't reset when you reload.
Every one of those things has a name. Trespassing. Theft of services. A traffic violation.
And thanks to Mo's video, every single one of them has evidence. In high definition.
Then you hear it. A siren. Getting closer.
